```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>")
library(agecraft)
library(dplyr)
library(tibble)
```

An age workflow connects three tasks: calculate ages from dates, define the age intervals you need fir grouping, and
categorize each age into an age group. A scheme adds purpose and provenance to an interval definition when those choices
need to travel with an analysis.

In the first 'quick" we'll work through a short example using age in completed years and quick group definitions. The
second section provides a more detailed description an steps by developing a report workflow that keeps fractional ages,
reviews date problems, documents a scheme, and produces a frequency table of age groups with the information needed to
interpret and reproduce it.

## A quick age workflow

### Calculate ages in completed years

Suppose each row is one person's visit. Choose the visit date as the reference
for age and calculate completed years:

```{r quick-ages}

# Create the visits tibble and calculate ages.
visits <- tibble(
  birth_date = as.Date(c("2020-01-16", "2020-01-15", "2000-08-20", "1960-01-15")),
  visit_date = as.Date("2025-01-15")
) |>
  mutate(
    age_at_visit = calculate_age(birth_date, visit_date, unit = "year"),
    age_years = as.integer(age_at_visit)
  )

visits
```

The ages are 4, 5, 24, and 65 completed years. The tibble shows the `age`
class and year unit beneath the `age_at_visit` column name; `age_years` is an
ordinary integer column. `as.integer()` explicitly keeps
the age in completed years only. That is sufficient for the whole-year cut points below;
keep the default `age` result when fractions or unit metadata will matter later.

### Categorize with a preset or your own cut points

Use the supplied five-year cut points for a quick classification:

```{r quick-preset}
visits <- visits |>
  mutate(five_year_group = categorize_age(age_years, by = age_interval_presets$Yr.5))
visits |> select(age_years, five_year_group)
```

The numeric ages and cut points are both interpreted here as years. Presets
are historical reporting conventions; choose one because its boundaries suit
your task, rather than assuming its name establishes an official standard.

For your own cut points, supply the boundaries directly:

```{r quick-cut-points}
visits <- visits |>
  mutate(broad_group = categorize_age(age_years, by = c(0, 18, 65, Inf)))
visits |> select(age_years, broad_group)
```

These intervals are `[0, 18)`, `[18, 65)`, and `[65, Inf)`: the lower boundary
is included, and the upper boundary is excluded. Someone exactly 65 belongs
to the final group. `Inf` gives the last group no finite upper limit.

If you want to name and reuse those intervals, make an `age_interval` vector:

```{r quick-named-intervals}
broad_intervals <- age_interval(breaks = c(0, 18, 65, Inf), unit = "year")
names(broad_intervals) <- c("Under 18", "18–64", "65+")
visits <- visits |>
  mutate(broad_group = categorize_age(age_at_visit, by = broad_intervals))
visits |> select(age_at_visit, broad_group)
```

Here we use the original `age_at_visit` column, which already carries its year
unit and stored fractions. Its unit matches the interval definition. `categorize_age()` returns an `age_group`
with ordered categories and their interval definitions. This completes a quick
calculate–define–categorize workflow. The following section carries those same
steps into an analysis where precision, missing data, and documentation matter.

## An age workflow for an analysis

We will prepare a frequency table of age groups for illness episodes with onset
in January 2025. Each row is one episode, so the frequencies count episodes,
not necessarily distinct people. Alongside the table, we will retain the
record-level assignments, date-review counts, and scheme definition.

### Decide what each record and its age represent

Each record has a unique ID. Assume that case eligibility and duplicate checks
have already been completed, apart from the unresolved dates we review below.

```{r records}
# Create the example tibble.
records <- tibble(
  record_id = sprintf("E%02d", 1:10),
  birth_date = as.Date(c(
    "2020-01-16", "2020-01-15", "2010-06-01", "2000-08-20",
    "1960-01-15", "1939-09-01", NA, "2025-02-01",
    "1985-04-10", "2021-01-10"
  )),
  onset_date = as.Date(c(
    rep("2025-01-15", 8), NA, "2025-01-20"
  )),
  report_date = as.Date(c(
    rep("2025-01-22", 8), "2025-01-23", "2025-02-03"
  ))
)
records
```
For this report, age will be defined as **age at symptom onset**, and inclusion
in the month is based on onset date. A report date answers a different question:
when the record reached the reporting system. An example of onset and reporting
months is E10 where the onset was in January whereas the report month is
February. E09 has no onset date, so we cannot establish its onset month or age
at onset from these fields.

The difference between using age at onset or age at report can also change the
age group assigned. E01 turns five between onset and reporting; E02 is already
five on the onset date. For example:

```{r event-choice}
records |>
  slice(1:2) |>
  transmute(
    record_id,
    age_at_onset = calculate_age(birth_date, onset_date, unit = "year"),
    age_at_report = calculate_age(birth_date, report_date, unit = "year")
  )
```
Using report date as a substitute for missing onset would mix two definitions of
age. We will retain the missing onset for review instead. A real reporting
protocol may specify a fallback date or a derived event date; document that rule
before applying it.

Retain the original dates if your analysis uses a derived date. This example
uses onset alone throughout.

### Separate date problems before calculating ages

A missing date and a birth date after onset both prevent a usable age, but they
call for different follow-up. Keep that distinction in a record-level status
variable. The checks below give missing birth dates priority when several
problems occur in the same record.

```{r date-review}
records <- records |>
  mutate(date_status = case_when(
    is.na(birth_date) ~ "Missing birth date",
    is.na(onset_date) ~ "Missing onset date",
    birth_date > onset_date ~ "Birth after onset",
    TRUE ~ "Ready"
  ))
records |> count(date_status, name = "records")

# Display the records where there is a date problem.
records |>
  filter(date_status != "Ready") |>
  select(record_id, birth_date, onset_date, date_status)
```
E07 needs a birth date, E08 needs its birth or onset date sequence corrected,
and E09 needs an onset date. We will keep all three records in the audit trail
without assigning them an age group. We cannot infer a correction from these
values alone.

```{r calculate-ages}
reviewed_ages <- records |>
  filter(date_status == "Ready") |>
  transmute(
    record_id,
    age_at_onset = calculate_age(birth_date, onset_date, unit = "year")
  )
records <- records |>
  left_join(reviewed_ages, by = "record_id")
```
Only the reviewed date pairs enter `calculate_age()`. Reversed pairs would
otherwise return missing ages and issue a warning under its default policy.
The review gives those missing results a reason we can carry into the report.

We calculate calendar years. For February 29 births, the default anniversary in
non-leap years is March 1; use `leap_day = "feb28"` if that is your reporting
rule. Record this choice with the analysis. Printing shows completed years,
but the calculated ages retain fractions.

### Keep fractional ages until the groups are assigned

The quick workflow used completed years. For whole-year boundaries, discarding
the fraction does not change membership: both 4 and 4.9 belong below 5. But an
integer no longer tells us how far someone has progressed through that year.
That matters when a boundary falls within a year.

```{r fractional-ages}
records |>
  filter(date_status == "Ready") |>
  transmute(
    record_id,
    completed_years = as.integer(age_at_onset),
    fractional_years = round(as.numeric(age_at_onset), 4)
  )
```

E01 is just short of five at onset; E02 is exactly five. The `age` display uses
completed years, while the stored values keep that distinction. Rounding here
is only for inspection; pass the original ages to classification.

For a short illustration of a fractional boundary, compare two ages around
4.5 years:

```{r fractional-boundary}
example_ages <- age(c(4.4, 4.6), unit = "year")
half_year_intervals <- age_interval(breaks = c(0, 4.5, Inf), unit = "year")
tibble(
  stored_years = as.numeric(example_ages),
  using_fractions = categorize_age(example_ages, by = half_year_intervals),
  after_truncating = categorize_age(
    age(as.integer(example_ages), unit = "year"), by = half_year_intervals
  )
)
```

The stored ages belong to different groups. Truncating both to 4 puts them in
the lower group and loses the information needed to recover the assignment.
Keep fractions when you may need finer boundaries later. If the analysis needs
calendar months, calculate age in months from the dates rather than assuming
a fixed number of days per month or an exact conversion from fractional years.

### Move from preset cut points to documented definitions

The quick example used `age_interval_presets$Yr.5`, a numeric vector of cut
points. Numeric presets use the ages' unit; they do not carry their own unit or
source metadata. An `age_interval` adds explicit bounds, a unit, and optional
category names. An `age_scheme` contains those intervals together with their
purpose and provenance.

The registry offers scheme versions of the historical presets:

```{r preset-scheme}
five_year_scheme <- get_age_scheme("legacy_yr_5")
scheme_intervals(five_year_scheme)
five_year_scheme[c("id", "source", "version", "verified")]

records |>
  transmute(
    record_id,
    five_year_group = categorize_age(age_at_onset, by = five_year_scheme)
  )
```

These schemes declare years and record the known source history. They are
unverified legacy definitions, not claims of current institutional authority.
Check the applicable specification before adopting one. For this report we
will instead document our own illustrative boundaries and the reason for them.

### Document reusable age groups with an age scheme

An `age_scheme` contains named age intervals together with descriptive metadata
and provenance. Use `age_scheme()` when a definition needs to be reused or
explained beyond the current calculation. For the `age_scheme` class model, see [The age_scheme
class](v03-classes.html#the-age_scheme-class-a-reusable-definition-with-context).

A saved scheme lets later reports reuse the same intervals, labels and unit,
while carrying their source, version and purpose. Supplying that scheme to
`categorize_age()` applies its intervals; it does not attach all of the scheme's
metadata to each assignment. Keep the scheme with the analysis.

Our illustrative report uses six age groups covering all ages in
years. A single scheme keeps the named intervals together with the purpose and
source of the definition. You can replace these groups with the applicable specification
in a real reporting system.

```{r reporting-scheme}
reporting_intervals <- age_interval(breaks = c(0, 5, 18, 45, 65, 85, Inf), unit = "year")
names(reporting_intervals) <- c("Under 5", "5–17", "18–44", "45–64", "65–84", "85+")
reporting_scheme <- age_scheme(
  reporting_intervals,
  id = "example_onset_report",
  name = "Illustrative onset reporting age groups",
  type = "partition",
  domain = c(0, Inf),
  purpose = "Count illness episodes by age at symptom onset",
  source = "Synthetic example in the age workflow vignette",
  version = "Teaching example 1",
  notes = "Not an official surveillance classification; ages measured in years."
)
scheme_intervals(reporting_scheme)
```
The age intervals include the lower bound and exclude the upper bound. Under 5 in
interval notation means `[0, 5)` years, and 5–17 means `[5, 18)`. E02 belongs to
5–17 on its fifth birthday. E01 remains Under 5 at onset, even though its age at
report would put it in the next age group.

### Check coverage before counting

To produce additive counts, we need both complete coverage of our intended age
domain and non-overlapping age groups. Check these independently.

```{r coverage-check}
coverage <- summary(reporting_scheme)
coverage[c("domain", "domain_inferred", "complete", "overlaps")]
coverage$gaps
stopifnot(isTRUE(coverage$complete), !coverage$overlaps)
```
The domain (ages covered) is explicitly `[0, Inf)` years, completeness is TRUE,
and overlaps are FALSE: these age groups form a partition of that domain. An
explicit domain makes our intended coverage part of the check. The `age_scheme`
constructor with `type = "partition"` rejects interval overlap but permits gaps,
so the completeness check still matters.

Overlapping age interval definitions can be valid schemes for other purposes. Selecting the first match would
resolve a software ambiguity, but would not establish a justified reporting rule. For intentionally overlapping
memberships, see [Creating and using reusable age schemes](v07-age-schemes.html).

### Assign age groups and account for every record

We can now classify the ages using the documented scheme. Explicitly requiring
matching units avoids a conversion during this step.

```{r assign-groups}
records <- records |>
  mutate(
    age_group = categorize_age(
      age_at_onset, by = reporting_scheme,
      multiple = "error", convert_units = "none"
    ),
    report_status = case_when(
      date_status != "Ready" ~ date_status,
      is.na(age_group) ~ "Age outside reporting groups",
      TRUE ~ "Included"
    )
  )
records |> select(record_id, age_at_onset, age_group, report_status)
```
A missing assignment alone cannot tell us whether dates were missing, dates were
invalid, or a usable age fell outside the definition. `report_status` preserves
those explanations. With these complete age groups, none of the seven usable
ages should be outside the definition.

```{r record-accounting}
accounting <- records |>
  count(status = report_status, name = "records")
accounting
stopifnot(sum(accounting$records) == nrow(records))
```
Seven records are included and three need date review. The missing-onset record
also has unresolved reporting-period eligibility. Keep these review counts
alongside the frequency table; omitting missing assignments silently would hide why
only seven of the ten input records contribute.

### Build a frequency table of age groups

The `age_group` result retains all defined levels, including age groups with no
observations. `count(..., .drop = FALSE)` therefore includes the empty 45–64 age
group. A zero means no included episodes in that age group; it does not mean the
definition was absent.

```{r reporting-table}
age_report <- records |>
  filter(report_status == "Included") |>
  count(age_group, name = "episodes", .drop = FALSE)
age_report
stopifnot(sum(age_report$episodes) == sum(records$report_status == "Included"))
```
The frequency table has two episodes Under 5, two aged 5–17, one aged 18–44, none aged
45–64, one aged 65–84, and one aged 85 or older. These counts sum to the seven
included records. Retain `records` for record-level review and
`reporting_scheme` for the boundaries and provenance: the assignment vector
alone does not retain the original ages or the scheme's provenance.

### Choose intervals that answer the analysis question

A frequency table of age groups depends on the boundaries chosen. Our Under 5
group pools infants with children aged 1–4; that may be too broad if infancy is
central to the question. Five-year bands and broad child/adult groups preserve
different distinctions even when applied to the same records. Labels alone do
not establish that two reports used the same bounds or units.

See [Choosing age groups for an analysis](v06-age_scheme_selection.html) for a
worked comparison of schemes, what pooling can conceal, and how denominator
availability and precision affect the choice. A scheme records that decision;
its validation does not establish that the decision suits the analysis.

### Interpret counts before calculating rates

The table describes the age distribution of included episodes in this example. A
larger count in one age group does not by itself imply greater disease risk: the
population in that age group may also be larger. Population rates need
appropriate denominators for the same geography, period, age-attribution rules
and age groups, with a numerator that matches the rate's definition. The records
needing date review can also affect the apparent age distribution.

Before using external population counts, check their units, boundaries and
coverage against the reporting scheme. A denominator for ages 0–9 cannot be
split into Under 5 and 5–9 from interval overlap alone. Likewise, overlapping
categories cannot be summed as if each person appeared exactly once. See
[Comparing age intervals](v08-age-range-comparisons.html) for what crosswalks
can establish and where additional data or assumptions are needed.

### Cite the scheme used in the analysis

The frequency table uses `reporting_scheme`, so that is the definition to cite.
Export its recorded metadata with the standard `utils::toBibtex()` generic:

```{r scheme-citation}
scheme_citation <- reporting_scheme |> utils::toBibtex()
scheme_citation
```

The result is a BibTeX `@Misc` entry whose key is the scheme ID,
`example_onset_report`. Its title, source, version, purpose, and notes identify
the definition used. Unknown reference information remains explicit; export
does not invent an author or publication year or verify the source. Here the
entry identifies our synthetic teaching definition, not an official standard.

For a published scheme, record its actual source, reference, and edition before
exporting the citation. Cite the scheme used, including any documented
adaptation, rather than only the name of a preset. The citation supplies
bibliographic context; keep the scheme object as well to preserve its exact
intervals. Package attribution is separate and is available through
`citation("agecraft")`.

### Keep the frequency table and its documentation together

The seven included episodes are accounted for in the frequency table; three
records remain available for date review. The assignments retain interval
definitions, but they do not retain the scheme's provenance or the original
ages. Keep those objects together rather than relying on a printed table alone.

```{r analysis-bundle}
analysis_result <- list(
  frequency_table = age_report,
  record_accounting = accounting,
  records = records,
  scheme = reporting_scheme,
  scheme_citation = scheme_citation,
  age_calculation = list(
    reference = "Symptom onset date; no fallback for missing onset",
    unit = "year",
    leap_day = "mar1",
    period = "January 2025"
  ),
  package_version = as.character(utils::packageVersion("agecraft"))
)
analysis_result$scheme[c("id", "name", "purpose", "source", "version", "notes")]
```

The bundle keeps the frequency table beside the data, the exact intervals,
their purpose and source, and the age calculation choices. To retain the R
objects between sessions, save the bundle with `saveRDS()`; a CSV export of the
frequency table alone will not preserve that context.

```{r save-analysis, eval=FALSE}
saveRDS(analysis_result, "age-workflow-result.rds")
writeLines(as.character(scheme_citation), "age-workflow-scheme.bib")
```

These save calls are not run during vignette rendering because they write files
for your analysis. The `.bib` file can be used in a report bibliography. Choose
an appropriate project location when saving either file.

For more on assignments, see [Working with assigned age groups](v05-age-groups.html).
For source metadata and later adaptations of a definition, continue with
[Creating and using reusable age schemes](v07-age-schemes.html).
